rationale: A plastic card face that a hidden projector rewrites to show any value is a remotely rewritable surface, but by light projection for cheating, not an electronically updated reading display.

A robot rolling across grass in back-and-forth strips and shifting sideways its own width is the boustrophedon coverage pattern of a robotic mower; the quote shows no cutting, though, and the context is unspecified.
A mural typographical map on a wall is a large 2D/3D-looking display of regional data; it is not a volumetric display viewable from several sides, so it only points loosely toward 3D visualization.
Machines each controlled by a computer copying a human mind describe automated production, but the quote offers no lights-out operation or robots building robots, only mind-copy controllers.

A prototype computer supplying circuit equations and shaping the final design of its giant successor matches computers designing computers and CAD of circuits; the opacity-to-builders context differs from GM's design of car parts.
A slate that changes color and shows lines of characters at a button press is a reusable electronic display acting as a book, matching the e-paper reader; the color-change mechanism is vague.

Feeding a new course into the ship's computers and the ship responding matches computer-set navigation courses, but the quote gives no calculation of orbits or burns, and hyper-flight context differs.
A dictatyper used to compose a letter points toward dictation typing, but the quote only mentions it falling over and says nothing of speech recognition; it is a loose evocation.

Fully automatic factories making spare parts so a system is self-sufficient match lights-out factories in function; no mechanism is described and it is military and self-sustaining rather than a robot plant.
A helmet placed on a man to learn the whereabouts of someone gestures at memory extraction, but the quote reports only confusing results; far from decoding imagined visual patterns with fMRI.

A self-activating problem-seeking computer with senses and actuators matches a machine that pursues science autonomously, as Adam did; the mechanism is only described generically and it acts through bodies.
A machine remotely connected to your mind is a vague hint of thought control; no signal, interface or cursor-type control is described, so it only loosely evokes a BCI.

Machinery handling electrical equipment with no one driving it, not a soul, matches unattended automated operation; context is unloading and assembling a facility rather than a lights-out robot-building plant.

A robot attuned to thought waves that obeys the user matches thought-controlled machines in function; no mechanism of reading signals is given, and a real BCI controlled a cursor, not an autonomous robot.

A glowing, moving three-dimensional panorama of the Solar System matches a 3D volumetric display of a scene viewable in depth; the mechanism is unstated and context is astronomy rather than medical planning.
A thinkwriter that types while the man watches is a self-typing machine, but the quote shows a form slid in and typing with no hint of reading thoughts; evocative only.
The brain's electromagnetic vibration telling a story, read by a refined EEG, matches reading mental content from brain activity; the 2006 decoding was fMRI of visual patterns, a narrower result.
Needles in the wrists connecting to a ship computer give a direct body-to-computer link, but through wrist tubes punching data from instruments, not decoding brain signals.
A Hypno-Mech Tape Library is only a place name suggesting hypnotic recorded teaching; no lesson played during sleep is described, so it only loosely points at sleep learning.
A mind-linked device responsive to thought through invisible tracts matches control of a machine by the mind; the nerve-like link is unspecified and no signal is read or decoded.
A machine that learned a person's language, thoughts and name matches mind reading in function; no mechanism is stated and extracting language is more than the fMRI pattern decoding achieved.

A galvanometer-based psychometer that gets truth from patients by detecting involuntary reactions matches the polygraph's physiological-signal deception detection; the medical-use context differs from police use.

A door that opens when a scanner recognizes fingerprints from a hand on a screen matches automated fingerprint authentication; the real 1965 milestone was computerized analysis for AFIS, not door locks.
A probe that would save time over taped debriefing implies extracting agent memories, yet the quote only names an expensive installation; no mechanism, just a hint of mind reading.
A combined calculating machine and typewriter producing accounts and invoices matches automating clerical work as LEO did; the mechanism is a single device, not a general computer.
Gadgets that took care of themselves is a brief hint of automatic operation; recording instruments are not a factory and there is no manufacturing or robots.
A cybernetic brain controlling quality regulators across all factories suggests centralized automated control of production, but quality regulation is not a self-running plant.
An inflated transparent globe four feet across hints at a 3D projection volume, but the quote shows only the inflation and no volumetric imagery; loose.
A glowing plate on which palms are placed for scanning matches automated print reading by a scanner; the fingerprint matching mechanism is not stated and it is not AFIS database matching.
A radio-controlled table governed by Mel evokes remote device control, but radio control is not a brain signal interface; the quote lacks any brain impulses.
Robots once controlled telepathically gives the function of mind-controlled machines but with no mechanism and no implant or signal; evocative only.
A corporation turning out thousands of industrial robots matches the robot manufacturing industry that Unimation began; the quote is generic, with Earth and Mars context.
A machine that tunes in on thought waves like a television matches mind reading with a broadcast-receiver analogy; mechanism is vague and the real decoding used fMRI.
Fully automatic Lensmakers needing no maintenance are self-running machines, but they make telepathic lenses, not goods in a robot factory; thin match.

A machine giving a perfect illusion of reality in three dimensions touching all senses matches immersive VR in function; the real 1990 systems used a head-mounted display and glove with limited senses.
A cap that reads a visualized world and shows it on a screen matches thought display and brain interfacing; the instant transport and the 1998 cursor control differ in mechanism.
An electrode on the head that reads a witness's memory of a face and prints a sketch matches decoding of visual content from brain activity; electrode versus fMRI differs.
A three-dimensional model of space where a new red dot appears evokes a 3D tracking display, with no mechanism or medium described; loosely related.
Information from a mind via helmet pickups translated into English matches thought-to-text in function; the mechanism is asserted but the real work decoded images, not text.
Thought images thrown on a screen from a subject matches displaying a person's mental images; mechanism is unstated, and the 2006 reconstructed simple visual patterns.
Robots scanning envelope addresses photoelectrically and sorting them into slots match optical character recognition for mail sorting; the robot context differs from a post office reader.
Machines to run the machines hints at self-maintaining automation, but the line is a remark with no factory or operation described.
A lawn-tender that crept out of a kennel to see if grass needed cutting matches autonomous mowing with dock and sensing; watering and its home-garden context differ from the 1969 MowBot.
Millions of hidden microphones routed to a central computer that screens speech match automated mass eavesdropping with keyword screening, as ECHELON did; it is a domestic street-level system.
A sleep-learner headband worn while studying matches teaching during sleep in function; the oscillator mechanism does not match played word-pair recordings, and there is no sleep detail.
A continuously changing 3D star map making the wall seem a miniature universe matches a 3D display viewable in depth; mechanism is unspecified and it appears on a wall.
An abstract concept hurled into the machine to find a listing matches thought-controlled operation; the mechanism is unspecified and it is not a decoded cursor signal.

Radar speeds and sizes fed into a calculator with the ship on automatic tracking match computer-assisted navigation in function; Gemini used a computer for orbit and reentry guidance, a different task.
